items.title: France Is Blaming Iran for the Fridge Cyberattack
items.description: Interesting: U.S. intelligence agencies have recently reached a “”ow confidence” assessment that Iran was responsible for the attacks in France, according to three U.S. officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence. A “low confidence” assessment generally means that there is some intelligence that points in a certain direction but is fragmented, and that the assessment could change as more information is collected. The agencies’ judgment on the French incidents linked those attacks to Iran generally and not to a specific group such as the Revolutionary Guards, two of the officials said. They added that Iran was also seen as probably responsible for other similar attacks around Europe, but that those investigations were in their early stages. Alternate link.

items.title: Formal Verification of the Signal Protocol Using AI
items.description: This seems like a good thing: Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees­a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. […] The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work. Alternate link. Details: First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human ­ just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Technical paper.

items.title: Critical Java Vulnerability Requires Immediate Patching
items.description: Purpose CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution. Actions to take CISA urges organizations to take the following actions: Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories. Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems. If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access. Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions. Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing. I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind. Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. items.title: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition
items.description: Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient. LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster. LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior. Patch soak time is no longer meaningful in a world where attackers can almost immediately determine bug details from a patch, and can put users at risk by creating a false sense of secrecy. “Patch gap” is the time between a fix being released for a security vulnerability and the user installing the relevant update. It is equally crucial that vendors reduce patch gap, either by reducing patch rollout time or using other strategies to protect users while remediation is in progress. LLMs have also increased the volume of vulnerabilities that Project Zero reports. We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year. Aspects of our policy that require vendor negotiation or agreement, including determining whether a bug is fixed and whether grace period applies, are quickly becoming unmanageable. items.title: VU#644655: TightVNC and UltraVNC Viewer contains a heap-based buffer overflow
items.description: Overview A heap-based buffer overflow exists in the Tight JPEG decoding component of the TightVNC Windows Viewer version 1.3.10 and affected UltraVNC Windows Viewers. An attacker controlling a malicious VNC server can trigger memory corruption by sending a specially crafted screen update. Successful exploitation can crash the viewer and may allow arbitrary code execution, although only denial of service conditions were demonstrated during testing. Description TightVNC and UltraVNC provide remote desktop access using the Remote Framebuffer (RFB) protocol. Their viewer applications connect to VNC servers and decode screen updates for local display. Tight encoding supports JPEG compression of image data within these updates. The Windows viewer function DecompressJpegRect() allocates a heap buffer using a hardcoded maximum row width of 8,192 pixels but converts JPEG pixel data using the server-supplied rectangle width without adequately checking that the output fits within the buffer. A malicious server can supply an oversized Tight JPEG rectangle that causes the conversion loop to write beyond the allocated memory. In an allocation demonstrated during testing, which included 256 bytes of padding, the out-of-bounds write began at a rectangle width of 8,257 pixels. Exploitation requires a vulnerable viewer to establish a session with an attacker-controlled or compromised VNC server and process its crafted update. The server can advertise a sufficiently large framebuffer, so checking that the rectangle fits within the advertised framebuffer does not, by itself, prevent this overflow. Authentication or transport encryption does not prevent exploitation by a malicious server participating in the session. Impact An attacker controlling a VNC server can corrupt heap memory in a connected vulnerable viewer, terminating the application and interrupting the remote desktop session. Collectively referred to as ImageTragick2, these issues arise when ImageMagick processes attacker-controlled SVG or PostScript content using dangerous coders or delegates permitted by its default or application-supplied configuration. An attacker who can upload an image, or otherwise cause an application to process crafted image content, may be able to read or write files accessible to the ImageMagick process. In some deployments, these capabilities may be chained to achieve arbitrary code execution, compromising the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the affected application and host. items.title: VU#685399: PromZard context key code injection leads to remote code execution
items.description: Overview The npm library promzard, versions 4.0.0 and earlier, is vulnerable to remote code execution due to direct string interpolation of context object keys, which allows unsanitized JavaScript code injection. Description promzard is a Node.js library designed to automate configuration workflows by evaluating template modules and generating data objects via interactive prompting. The library allows users to provide a context object ctx to expose specific data to the template module. promzard builds an object by walking the template module for prompt() and asynchronous functions. The keys of ctx, however, are treated as raw JavaScript source code instead of inert data. The implementation performs direct string interpolation of ctx keys, without validation or sanitization, into the parameter list of a function-expression source string that is then evaluated with vm.runInThisContext(). A key containing attacker-controlled JavaScript syntax can be executed during evaluation. Impact An attacker capable of influencing the ctx object’s keys (e.g. via parsed configuration file, an HTTP request, or environment variables) can break out of the function parameter list and inject arbitrary JavaScript code. This results in remote code execution within the context of the Node.js process. Solution Unfortunately, the maintainers of promzard could not be reached to coordinate the vulnerability. The CERT/CC recommends users ensure that any data used to populate ctx is strictly validated, and that arbitrary keys should not be passed from untrusted sources. Acknowledgements Thanks to Abdullah Hamdan for reporting this vulnerability. This document was written by Alex Lewis. items.description: Overview ComfyUI-Easy-Use version 1.4.1 and earlier contains a vulnerability in its save_preview() handler that allows an unauthenticated attacker to overwrite an installed custom node’s Python file. An attacker who can reach the affected ComfyUI instance over the network can use the overwrite to execute arbitrary code when ComfyUI restarts. Description ComfyUI is a node-based interface for building generative AI workflows. ComfyUI-Easy-Use is an extension that adds custom nodes and workflow utilities. save_preview() to copy that file over an installed custom node’s __init__.py. Upon restart, ComfyUI will import and execute the modified node. Remote exploitation requires a deployment that exposes the affected routes to the attacker without authentication. Impact An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the affected routes can execute arbitrary Python code and operating system commands with the privileges of the ComfyUI process. The attacker can read or modify models, workflows, and other files accessible to the process and obtain credentials available in its environment. Exploitation requires no user interaction. The reporter confirmed the vulnerability in ComfyUI-Easy-Use version up to verion 1.4.1. Solution Unfortunately, the maintainer of ComfyUI-Easy-Use could not be reached to coordinate this vulnerability. items.description: Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers used codename MDASH to investigate Linux kernel vulnerabilities, resulting in 59 upstream bug reports, 33 assigned CVEs, and 38 merged fixes. The research includes eight demonstrated local root privilege-escalation exploits and examines the challenges of turning AI-generated findings into validated vulnerabilities and upstream fixes. The post Lessons from 59 Linux Kernel Bug Reports appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
